history.heading: A principality is born
paragraphs: Liechtenstein, a small Alpine country between Switzerland and Austria, takes its name from the princely House of Liechtenstein, an Austrian noble family. In 1699 and 1712 the family bought the lordships of Schellenberg and Vaduz, and in 1719 the Holy Roman Emperor united them as the Principality of Liechtenstein.
Liechtenstein became sovereign in 1806 and fully independent after the dissolution of the German Confederation in 1866. It abolished its army in 1868 and remained neutral in both world wars.

history.heading: Close ties with Switzerland
paragraphs: After the First World War, Liechtenstein turned from Austria to Switzerland, forming a customs union in 1923 and adopting the Swiss franc. Prince Franz Joseph II moved to Vaduz in 1938, the first ruling prince to live there permanently. From a poor agricultural country, Liechtenstein became one of the richest in the world after 1945.

culture.heading: Alpine culture
paragraphs: German is the official language, and an Alemannic dialect is spoken in daily life. Most people are Catholic. About a third of residents are foreign nationals. The princely family's art collection is one of the most important private collections in the world. Vaduz Castle, the prince's residence, overlooks the capital.

politics.heading: Constitutional monarchy
paragraphs: Liechtenstein is a constitutional monarchy in which the reigning prince holds significant powers, including vetoing laws and dismissing the government, strengthened by a 2003 referendum. Prince Hans-Adam II handed day-to-day duties to his son, Hereditary Prince Alois, in 2004.
The Landtag (parliament) is elected, and Liechtenstein has strong direct democracy through referendums. It is a member of the European Economic Area and Schengen but not the EU.

economy.heading: Industry and finance
paragraphs: Liechtenstein has one of the world's highest GDPs per person. Surprisingly for its size, it has a strong industrial sector, including precision manufacturing, dental products (Ivoclar) and tools (Hilti). Financial services are also important, and after tax scandals the country moved away from banking secrecy.
More people commute into Liechtenstein for work each day than live there. The currency is the Swiss franc.
